where: Section 2, paragraph after the tan β formula
problem: The sentence is broken: "When the v-plane is the more flexible one, I_v  θ, so the tip swings away from the load line towards v." A number, the comparison and the inequality have dropped out, so a student cannot tell what condition makes β exceed θ.
fix: When the v-plane is the more flexible one, I_v < I_u, so I_u/I_v > 1 and β > θ; the tip swings away from the load line towards v.

problem: The arithmetic is written as "6400 / 8.40 × 10⁵ = 7.62 × 10⁻³ m". Read left to right as printed this gives 7.62 × 10⁵, not 7.62 × 10⁻³. The denominator is not bracketed, so a student copying the line gets a nonsensical answer.

where: Section 1, definitions of I_u and I_v
problem: The labels follow the plane, not the axis: I_u here means the second moment that governs bending in the u–z plane, which is the moment about the v axis (∫u² dA). Most textbooks, and the stress formula of Chapter 4.2, write I_u for the second moment about the u axis (∫v² dA). A student carrying this page into 4.2 will pair the symbols wrongly.
fix: State the convention explicitly: "I_u is the second moment about the v axis, I_u = ∫u² dA, the value used in σ = M u / I_u for bending in the u–z plane; I_v = ∫v² dA is about the u axis. Some books swap these labels; check which one the formula is written with."

problem: "Other supports change only the constant in front" is imprecise: the deflected shape changes too (z²(3L − z)/(2L³) for a cantilever tip load, z(3L² − 4z²)/(48L³) for a central point load on a simple span). What stays true is that the two planes still share one shape, so the components still combine as vectors.
fix: Other supports change the coefficient and the shape in each plane, but both planes still share the same shape, so you resolve, take the tabulated deflection in each plane, and combine as vectors.
